title: Using Electoral Cycles in Police Hiring to Estimate the Effect of Police on Crime
research_question: Does an increase in the size of municipal police forces causally reduce crime rates, and if so, by how much do violent and property crimes respond to changes in police per capita?
data_description: The analysis uses a city-year panel of 59 large U.S. cities with directly elected mayors over 1970-1992. Key variables include annual growth rates in police officers per capita and growth rates in seven crime categories per capita: murder, rape, robbery, aggravated assault (violent crimes), and burglary, larceny excluding motor vehicle theft, and motor vehicle theft (property crimes). Additional covariates include city fixed effects, year indicators, region indicators, city-size indicators, and six state- and MSA-level controls (including state and local education and welfare spending). Timing of mayoral and gubernatorial elections is recorded as election-year indicators with one- and two-year lags. Police and crime data come largely from FBI Crime in the United States and ICPSR; mayoral election dates were recollected from the World Almanac and the Municipal Yearbook. The total sample comprises roughly 1,136 city-year observations per crime category.
institutional_context: U.S. municipal police forces are funded and staffed through local political processes, so incumbent mayors and governors facing reelection have incentives to expand visible public safety resources before voters go to the polls. This creates a recurring electoral cycle in police hiring: growth in officers per capita tends to be faster in years when mayors or governors stand for election than in off-cycle years, even though the underlying need for police should not move with the electoral calendar. Mayoral terms vary across the 59 cities studied, and gubernatorial terms vary across states, generating staggered timing of elections. Because politicians may also adjust hiring in response to anticipated crime waves, simple correlations between police levels and crime are confounded by simultaneity. The electoral calendar provides a source of variation in police staffing that is plausibly unrelated to contemporaneous crime trends, motivating its use to study how policing affects crime.
